notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Chodesh Adar II §1): “the Holy One said to him: I have no sleep before Me… and you said there is sleep before Me — by your life, from within "sleep" I rouse Myself over that man and destroy him, as it says,”and Hashem awoke as one asleep."" Exactly the se’if: what looks like a sealed and settled state is not settled at all — the very image of “sleep” is the one Scripture uses for a verdict that can still be roused and undone.

notes.body_html: Rosh Hashanah 17b: “R’ Yochanan said: Great is teshuvah, for it tears up a person’s [sealed] verdict, as it says (Yeshayah 6:10), ‘and his heart shall understand, and he shall repent, and it shall be healed for him.’ Rav Pappa said to Abbaye: perhaps [this is only] before the verdict [is sealed]? He answered: ‘and it shall be healed for him’ is written — what is a thing that requires healing? — say, that is a [sealed] verdict.”Shelah — direct kabbalistic background (Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Aseret HaDibrot, Rosh HaShanah, Torah Ohr §19): The Shelah identifies precisely the level that R' Tzadok places behind the phrase 'levavo yavin vashav.' The kelipos, he writes, obtain their hold around the sevenfold 'building' of the middos, but at Binah — the root from which that building issues — 'there is no touch of the outsider'; it is the secret of Olam Haba. 'Binah is called teshuvah, for there the emanation of the building returns.' When a person confesses, abandons the sin, repairs the damage and 'returns with all his heart,' he awakens that root of the building, 'and everything is purified, and the accuser departs, because there he has no hold.' This is an unusually exact background to the eighth rung described here. R' Tzadok's point is not merely that repentance persuades Heaven to cancel an externally imposed punishment. The heart's Binah reaches the root from which the lower structure and its dinim emerged; at that root the prosecuting hold is absent. Thus 've-rafa' can be described as a healing that has already taken place at the level of the heart itself, even before the full sevenfold actualization of teshuvah has been completed. The Shelah also helps explain why Rosh Hashanah is the natural setting for this teaching: the shofar awakens the lower person toward that root of Binah, while Yom Kippur completes and brings into actuality what was awakened in potential. R' Tzadok's grammatical distinction between 'erpa' and 've-rafa' therefore reflects two levels of one process — Divine completion from above, and a prior return of the damaged structure to the root in which its healing is already latent.

notes.body_html: Yoma 86a / Rashi: On “I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely” (Hoshea 14:5) — Rashi’s first explanation is that “I will heal” refers to a future healing, “like one blemished who was cured, upon whom part of his [former] name still rests.” R’ Tzadok leans on the grammar: erpa (“I will heal”) is a future act of God, whereas ve-rafa (“and he shall be healed”) is a completed, self-effected healing of the past.

notes.body_html: “Your right hand is outstretched to receive the penitent” (the Ne’ilah liturgy of Yom Kippur): in the closing service we declare, “You give a hand to transgressors, and Your right hand is outstretched to receive penitents” (yeminecha peshutah lekabel shavim) — that the sinner’s return is consummated when God, in His mercy, reaches out to receive him. Meforshim: the phrase distills the Sages’ portrayal of teshuvah’s welcome — the gates of return ever open, and the Holy One Himself drawing the penitent near. R’ Tzadok’s use: this is exactly the difficulty he presses — if teshuvah’s healing “requires His acceptance,” how can Scripture say “and he shall be healed [ve-rafa],” of itself? His answer: at its root (Rosh Hashanah — Binah in the heart) teshuvah already heals of itself, while its full actualization (Yom Kippur) is “what Hashem completes on his behalf and accepts.”

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Chodesh Adar §8): “the labor of this month is that even in sleep Israel are kuf — holy, since they are bound at the root in Hashem — and this accords with "I sleep [from the mitzvos] but my heart is awake [to do them]."” Exactly the se’if’s “ve-rafa”: the healing spoken of reaches a bond that never lapsed — the sleeping man was holy throughout, and therefore what is healed is genuinely the past.Izhbitz parallel — Mei HaShiloach I, Bereshit §6: The Mei HaShiloach calls the Etz HaChaim 'teshuvah amitiyos she-merape'os es ha-kodem' — true teshuvah that heals what came before — and then repeats the point with the river Peras: it waters the Tree of Life because it corresponds to baalei teshuvah, 'u-teshuvah merapei es ha-kodem,' healing even the deficiency that has accompanied a person from his earliest beginning and returning him to his first source. This makes R' Tzadok's close reading of 've-rafa' especially sharp. The Izhbitzer does not define teshuvah only as a new direction from now onward; its deepest form reaches the prior reality and changes the meaning of what preceded. That is exactly why R' Tzadok distinguishes the future-oriented 'erpa meshubasam' from 've-rafa' — already healed. Yet Mei HaShiloach also places the doctrine inside the image of the Tree of Life: the healing comes through return to the source of life, not through declaring the breach unreal while remaining where the breach occurred. The stronger the claim of retroactive healing, the stronger the implied demand of actual return. In the language of this se'if, the root-healing exists in the Binah of the heart, while the complete emergence of that healing into the seven lower middos still requires the Divine help and acceptance that carry the person's inward return into a finished life.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §87): "“He has not looked [with a fixed gaze]” — “iniquity in Yaakov”; a multitude in whom transgressions are frequent requires a fixed gaze in order to punish them — “and He has not seen,” with a mere glance, in Israel." Exactly the se’if: “I, Hashem, have not changed” describes His looking, not His mercy — the individual’s verdict stands because it was fixed by a gaze, and it is teshuvah itself that must do the tearing.

notes.body_html: Rosh Hashanah 17b–18a: After R’ Yochanan’s teaching that teshuvah tears up a verdict, the Gemara raises an objection and answers by distinguishing the individual from the community — an individual’s sealed verdict is not [automatically] torn, corresponding to “I, Hashem, have not changed” (Malachi 3:6), whereas a community’s is.Izhbitz on an apparently irrevocable Divine word — Mei HaShiloach II, Yonah 4:1: R. Mordechai Yosef gives a striking model for R' Tzadok's paradox of a verdict that is true and yet whose destructive effect can be removed without implying any change in God. Once a prophecy and Divine utterance has gone forth, the Mei HaShiloach says, 'it must necessarily accomplish something'; even if the people repent, 'this utterance does not return empty.' After Yonah had prophesied the overturning of Nineveh and Nineveh repented, Yonah still feared that some houses or streets would have to fall, because the prophetic word could not simply be false. Hashem therefore showed him the breadth of redemption: the entire operative force of the prophecy was discharged upon Yonah's kikayon. The word remained true, but its destructive application to the repentant city did not. This is an exceptionally useful Izhbitz complement to 'Ani Hashem lo shanisi.' Teshuvah is not a claim that Divine truth becomes untrue or that a sealed word is casually rescinded. Rather, return creates a new relation to the truth of that word, so that the person or community need no longer stand in the place upon which the din was written. R' Tzadok expresses this inwardly: the letters of the decree are formed from the sin and written in the heart; when the heart itself breaks and returns, the 'book' on which the decree was written is torn. The Izhbitzer expresses the same non-change from the side of prophecy: the word is not emptied, but mercy can redirect how its truth becomes actual. Neither teaching licenses presumption before the fact; both describe what becomes possible only when genuine teshuvah has changed the spiritual reality to which the decree had attached.

notes.body_html: The seven cleansing agents (Mishnah Niddah 9:6; Niddah 61b): “Seven substances remove a stain [kesem]: insipid saliva, bean-water, urine, natron [neser], borit, kimonia, and eshleg” — the fixed series by which the Sages test a suspected bloodstain. Meforshim: these are the most powerful launderers known to the Mishnah; and Rosh Hashanah 18a invokes two of them in expounding “though you wash with natron and use much borit, your iniquity is stained [nichtam] before Me” (Yirmeyah 2:22) — the stain of sin that no scouring removes. R’ Tzadok’s use: so too one “sunk in iniquity in all the depths of his heart” is like the “impure stain” that will not launder out “even if they pass over it all seven cleansing agents” — and this is the “sealing” of a verdict that cannot be torn, of which is said “none who come to her return” (Mishlei 2:19).

notes.body_html: Berachos 8a: “What is [the meaning of] ‘and as for me, my prayer is to You, Hashem, [at] an hour of favor’ (Tehillim 69:14)? When is an hour of favor? — when the community prays.” Communal prayer is inherently accepted, so it constitutes an “hour of favor” in which judgment gives way.Sefas Emes — the community itself generates the 'hour of favor' (Chukas 4:5): On 'va'ani sefilasi lecha Hashem es ratzon,' the Sefas Emes makes explicit the mechanism that R' Tzadok is deriving here. 'Bnei Yisrael awaken through their prayer an es ratzon,' he writes, citing the very teaching of Chazal, 'when is an hour of favor? when the community prays.' He reads the verse not merely as prayer taking advantage of a preexisting favorable moment, but as 'ha-tefillah goremes ha-ratzon' — the prayer causes the favor. There are, he adds, times when Hashem desires precisely that Israel should themselves bring forth this ratzon; the deepest Shabbos hour, ra'ava de-ra'avin, is a desire from above that Israel awaken desire from below. This maps almost exactly onto R' Tzadok's formulation that when the tzibbur awakens an es ratzon, there is automatically no place for din. The judgment need not be imagined as a decree that God first wills and then changes His mind about. A different Divine middah becomes the operative light because Knesses Yisrael, acting as a collective, has entered the relationship of ratzon. The Sefas Emes further says that on Shabbos Hashem has nachas from Creation through Israel's testimony to the Creator, and that this ratzon becomes the vitality of the coming week. R' Tzadok's phrase that Hashem is 'merutzeh be-olamo u-motzei naycha mi-beriyosav' is therefore not rhetorical ornament: Chassidic teaching treats the communal awakening of ratzon as a real source of renewed chiyus. The torn decree is the negative face of a positive event — the world has entered a state animated by favor rather than prosecution.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Vayeishev §3): “it is of the order of”a prayer of the poor man," who has nothing of his own — “I am with the crushed”; and this is what is said, “when you cry out, let your gatherings save you.”" Exactly the se’if: the cry that avails “both before and after the verdict” is the cry of one who claims nothing — which is why it operates by prayer and mercy rather than by right.R' Tzadok's later Chassidic development — Pri Tzadik, Shemos 8:1: Pri Tzadik develops the power of tze'akah in a way that clarifies why this se'if separates prayer and crying from teshuvah alone. On Israel's cry in Egypt, he cites the Zohar that 'tze'akah is greater than all of them, for tze'akah is in the heart,' and then: 'great is tze'akah, for it rules in this world and in the World to Come; through tze'akah a person inherits this world and the World to Come.' He identifies the two worlds with Malchus and Binah and returns to the same verse used throughout Takanas HaShavin: when fear penetrates to the depths of the heart, 'levavo yavin vashav' — Binah in the heart — becomes teshuvah ila'ah. The cry therefore reaches both the revealed order in which a decree operates and the higher root from which repair can flow. This is precisely why R' Tzadok here can preserve a real distinction between teshuvah and tze'akah without diminishing teshuvah. Teshuvah is the inward return of the heart; prayer and cry are the act by which that heart, stripped of self-sufficiency, turns directly to Hashem for rachamim. A sealed individual decree may remain fixed within the ordinary legal order, yet the cry can appeal from that order to the Source that encompasses both worlds. Pri Tzadik even applies this to those who appear spiritually lost or enclosed by kelipah, teaching that the 'great shofar' can awaken the root of return in the hidden heart. Thus 'yafah tze'akah bein kodem gezar din bein le'achar gezar din' is not an alternate technical loophole. It is a distinct mode of relation: instead of the sinner arguing that his inner change should itself erase the judgment, the broken heart cries to the One before whom both the judgment and the possibility of its merciful transcendence are present.

notes.body_html: Bereishis Rabbah 1:1: “‘And I was beside Him as an amon’ (Mishlei 8:30) — read uman [craftsman]: the Torah says, ‘I was the tool of craft [kli umanuso] of the Holy One.’ Just as a builder works from plans and tablets, so ‘the Holy One looked into the Torah and created the world.’” This is R’ Tzadok’s “blueprint of the Work of Creation”: since the world was made by means of the Torah, keeping its laws is what sustains the world.Izhbitz-Radzin — Torah is not an external code but the anatomy of life (Tiferet Yosef, Talmud Anthology, Chagigah §2): Tiferet Yosef develops the Zoharic principle 'Kudsha Berich Hu looked into the Torah and created the world' into exactly the ontology R' Tzadok requires in this se'if. The Torah, he explains, corresponds to the organs and joints of the human being; the 248 positive commandments and 365 prohibitions correspond to the limbs and sinews. A person whose desire is to remove concealment and see the Divine purpose within things can therefore discover Torah in his own created being — 'u-mi-besari echezeh Eloka' — because the world itself was formed through Torah. This is why Chazal compare Torah to the goad that directs an animal's furrow 'to bring life into the world': Torah directs its learners 'from the ways of death to the ways of life.' Tiferet Yosef then makes the consequence explicit. One who truly perceives the Torah within his own spiritual anatomy knows that severing himself from even one positive command or transgressing a prohibition is not merely disobeying an arbitrary order; it is a real disconnection from life. This is almost a Chassidic gloss on R' Tzadok's words that, were mitzvos only royal decrees, pardon should suffice, whereas in truth Torah is the 'blueprint of Creation' and the aveirah itself pursues the sinner. The punishment is not fundamentally retaliation added from outside; the Torah has disclosed which movements accord with the organism of Creation and which tear at it. Yet Tiferet Yosef also points toward teshuvah: the purpose of the struggle is to remove hester and come back to Divrei Torah, at which point even the road by which one reached them can be gathered into the Divine teaching. That final point preserves R' Tzadok's broader thesis: the objective structure of Torah is real, but return can reach a root deep enough to restore life to what had been severed.

notes.body_html: “By ten utterances the world was created” (Avos 5:1): “By ten utterances the world was created. And what does this teach — could it not have been created by a single utterance? Rather, to exact punishment from the wicked, who destroy the world created by ten utterances, and to give good reward to the righteous, who sustain the world created by ten utterances.” Meforshim: the Bartenura — the ten are the nine “and God said”s of Creation together with “In the beginning” (itself reckoned an utterance); the world is literally built by them, so that keeping or violating its order sustains or ruins it. R’ Tzadok’s use: “all this is only from the side of the laws Hashem inscribed in His world — the middos and utterances by which the world was made in the seven days” — by which the Torah’s laws “fence in” man; teshuvah, by contrast, “was created before the world,” standing above those very laws.Maharal — teshuvah as a pre-world foundation, not an exception to Creation (Netivos Olam, Netiv HaTeshuvah 4:13): The Maharal writes that teshuvah is not a contingent remedy introduced only after sin appeared: 'ha-teshuvah hi mi-yesodei ha-olam' — teshuvah is one of the foundations of the world. He proves this from Chazal's teaching that teshuvah was among the things created before the world, and adds a characteristic Maharalian principle: 'a thing that was created cannot fail to come into actuality, for otherwise its creation would be in vain.' This gives conceptual precision to R' Tzadok's insistence that the gates of teshuvah stand above the gates of the world's ordinary governance. If teshuvah were simply one more mechanism inside the created legal order, it would remain subject to that order's finalities — a broken law would generate its result and an irrevocable din would remain irrevocable. By placing teshuvah before the world, Chazal identify it as a principle by which the created order itself was founded with a path of return already built into its deepest design. The Maharal's formulation also prevents a common misunderstanding of 'above the laws.' Teshuvah is not lawlessness; it is itself a yesod established by Hashem prior to the differentiated world. Its transcendence of the world's boundaries is therefore part of Divine order at a more primordial level. This fits R' Tzadok's language exactly: the Torah's chukim correspond to the bounded middos and utterances of Creation, while the sinner who reaches the root of teshuvah reaches a prior level at which the breach of those boundaries does not define the whole of his being. The gates open because the possibility of return preceded the gate-system itself.

notes.body_html: Man, “a likeness of the world” (Midrash Tanchuma, Pekudei 3): the Midrash teaches that “the Tabernacle was equal to all the world and to the human embryo — which is a world in miniature,” for “the formation of the embryo is like the formation of the world.” Meforshim: this is the classic teaching that man is an olam katan — a microcosm — whatever the Holy One set in the great world He set, in small, in man. R’ Tzadok’s use: because man is “a likeness of the world,” the Torah’s laws — patterned on “the middos and utterances by which the world was created” — “fence in” man exactly as those laws bound and measure the world; so a sin is a breach of the very order of Creation, and “evil pursues sinners” of itself.

notes.body_html: Zohar, Shelach 161b: Just as the Holy One set the heart at the center of the body — the source of the whole body’s vitality, itself bound to the brain in the head — so He set Jerusalem at the center of the settled world, the Temple Mount within it, the courts within that, the Chamber of Hewn Stone, the altar, the Sanctuary, and innermost the Holy of Holies, “where the Shechinah, the Kapores, the Keruvim, and the Ark rest — and here is the heart of all the earth and the world,” from which all places are nourished.Earlier kabbalistic background — Sha'arei Orah, Gates Three–Four, §83: R. Yosef Gikatilla connects Binah, teshuvah, and the cancellation of a sealed decree with remarkable directness. Expounding 'es Mi no'atz va-yevineqhu,' he identifies the Divine name 'Mi' with Binah and calls it 'the place of teshuvah'; he then states: 'therefore, even though a verdict has been sealed above, Israel can annul it through the power of teshuvah that is called Mi.' This is valuable background to the entire movement of Siman 8 and especially to R' Tzadok's placement of the Holy of Holies, the heart, Binah and the gates of teshuvah in one structure. The ordinary verdict belongs to the articulated order of governance; Binah is the womb/root from which that articulation proceeds. To return there is not to overpower Divine judgment from outside but to reach the source at which judgment can be reconfigured within a higher unity. R' Tzadok's image of the Kodesh HaKodashim as 'liba de-kol ar'a ve-alma' adds an anthropological dimension to the same map: the person carries a corresponding hidden sanctuary in the depth of the heart, and 'levavo yavin vashav' is the inward movement toward that place. Sha'arei Orah thus supplies an older kabbalistic precedent for the very claim that might otherwise sound paradoxical: a sealed decree can remain genuinely sealed in the lower order while teshuvah, by ascending to Binah, reaches a level from which the decree can be undone. The cancellation is not a denial of the lower judgment but an appeal to its root.

This is valuable background to the entire movement of Siman 8 and especially to R' Tzadok's placement of the Holy of Holies, the heart, Binah and the gates of teshuvah in one structure. The ordinary verdict belongs to the articulated order of governance; Binah is the womb/root from which that articulation proceeds. To return there is not to overpower Divine judgment from outside but to reach the source at which judgment can be reconfigured within a higher unity. R' Tzadok's image of the Kodesh HaKodashim as 'liba de-kol ar'a ve-alma' adds an anthropological dimension to the same map: the person carries a corresponding hidden sanctuary in the depth of the heart, and 'levavo yavin vashav' is the inward movement toward that place. Sha'arei Orah thus supplies an older kabbalistic precedent for the very claim that might otherwise sound paradoxical: a sealed decree can remain genuinely sealed in the lower order while teshuvah, by ascending to Binah, reaches a level from which the decree can be undone. The cancellation is not a denial of the lower judgment but an appeal to its root.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §57): “for in every thing there are two extremes and a middle… and behold, the right itself is likewise divided into these three, as with everything bounded.” Exactly the se’if: the seven “building” days are an order of bounded things, each subdividing further — and Yom Kippur, “Shabbos Shabbason,” stands as the day that is not one of them.Tanya — the two heh's and the two levels of teshuvah (Iggeres HaTeshuvah, ch. 4): The Alter Rebbe opens his deeper explanation of teshuvah with the Zohar's reading of the word itself: 'tashuv hei' — the lower heh gives teshuvah tata'ah and the upper heh gives teshuvah ila'ah. He then maps the Divine Name in the same order used here by R' Tzadok: yud as the concealed point of Chochmah; the first heh as the expansion and revelation of Binah; vav as the downward extension through the six holy middos; and the final heh as Malchus and revealed speech. In the human soul, the same structure appears as concealed intellect, Binah and contemplation in the heart, the love and fear born from that understanding, and their final expression in Torah and mitzvos through speech and deed. This makes R' Tzadok's statement that Shabbos corresponds to the lower heh while Yom Kippur is the upper heh itself much more than a symbolic equivalence. The two heh's mark two locations of return within the same Divine-human structure. Teshuvah tata'ah restores the final, revealed level; teshuvah ila'ah returns the inner life toward the Binah from which the middos and their expression are born. It also explains why the Ten Days culminate on Yom Kippur. The tenth day is not merely the last date in a sequence but the disclosure of the upper root that can gather the differentiated lower levels back into one complete komah. R' Tzadok's 'Shabbos Shabbason' is therefore the Sabbath of the Sabbath: not only rest within the created order, but return of the created order toward its supernal mother-source.

notes.body_html: Vayikra 16:17: “וְכָל אָדָם לֹא יִהְיֶה בְּאֹהֶל מוֹעֵד בְּבֹאוֹ לְכַפֵּר בַּקֹּדֶשׁ עַד צֵאתוֹ” — “and no man shall be in the Tent of Meeting when he enters to make atonement in the Sanctuary, until he comes out.” Meforshim: Rashi, from the Sifra — “no man” excludes even those [angelic beings] “the likeness of whose face was a human face” (cf. Yechezkel 1:10); while the Kohen Gadol makes atonement within, no other being may be present — a place of utter concealment. R’ Tzadok’s use: the Holy of Holies, “the heart of the world,” stood “in the ultimate concealment”; so too teshuvah — though a genuine law of Creation — is hidden in this world, like the unfathomable heart into which only “Hashem searches.”Shelah on Yom Kippur as return of the branches to Binah (Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Aseret HaDibrot, Yoma, Torah Ohr §27): The Shelah gives an almost point-for-point parallel to the close of this siman. The first heh of the Divine Name is the supernal mother, he writes, and sin separates the mother from the children; 'great is teshuvah, for the mother returns upon her children — em ha-banim semechah.' 'There in Binah is the root of teshuvah,' and Binah is the secret of Olam Haba. The six upper days/middos are the children: they branch out from Binah and 'el ha-Binah shavim' — to Binah they return. For that reason a person must engage in teshuvah through the days of action and even on Shabbos, so that 'the branches return to their root.' This is precisely R' Tzadok's architecture of seven building days, a higher day, the upper heh, and a complete tenfold stature. The deepest function of Yom Kippur is therefore gathering: scattered acts, middos and days are not merely pardoned one by one; they are returned to the maternal root from which their life originally came. That also clarifies why the Kodesh HaKodashim and the heart are the matching coordinates in olam and nefesh. Both are hidden centers rather than exterior surfaces. The public world sees deeds after they have branched outward; Hashem 'searches the heart,' the concealed point in which their root can be understood and redirected. When R' Tzadok calls teshuvah itself one of the laws of Creation but says that it remains hidden in this world, the Shelah explains the paradox: it is indeed a law, but it is the law of the hidden root — Binah/Olam Haba — from which the visible sevenfold world continually issues and to which it is capable of returning.

notes.body_html: Pirkei d’Rabbi Eliezer 46 (Israel like the ministering angels): expounding Yom Kippur, the Midrash has the accuser Sammael concede before God — “You have one people like the ministering angels of heaven: just as the ministering angels have neither food nor drink, so Israel have neither food nor drink on the Day of Atonement; just as the ministering angels are barefoot, so Israel are barefoot; just as the ministering angels are innocent of all sin, so Israel are innocent of all sin on the Day of Atonement.” Meforshim: the classic reading — Israel’s fast and withdrawal from bodily need make them, for that day, like the angels who neither eat nor sin. R’ Tzadok’s use: “on Yom Kippur Israel resemble the ministering angels, withdrawing from every desire of this physical world” — the “concealment of physicality,” for “from the side of the body there is no access to the holiness of this day,” which is concealed in this world.
